mappings.note: Why grouping organisms matters -- it makes diversity studiable. The rationale for classification, LO-3.
Main characteristics of shrubs. Defines one of LO-3's own named plant classes.
Climbers versus creepers. Explicitly a difference on the basis of stem strength and growth habit, so LO-2 rather than the classification LO.
Explain parallel venation with an example. Describing an observable leaf feature and naming plants that show it, LO-1; no contrast with reticulate is asked.
What a taproot system is, plus an example. Identification of a structure from its observable form, LO-1.
The relationship between cotyledon number and venation type. Holds both sides of the monocot/dicot differentiation, LO-2.
Janaki Ammal documented and worked to preserve plant biodiversity and joined Save Silent Valley. Efforts to protect the environment, LO-11, rather than a bare biography.
Deodar's conical shape and sloping branches shed snow. Features explained by the demand of a snowy habitat, LO-5.
Fleshy cactus stems store water for dry conditions. A plant adaptation tied to habitat, LO-5.
Two differences between hot-desert and cold-desert camels. The item asks only for the differences, not their purpose, so LO-2 rather than LO-5.
How hot-desert camels conserve water -- concentrated urine, dry dung, little sweating. Features related to the demand of the habitat, LO-5.
Define habitat with an example. Habitat as the organising frame for sorting organisms, LO-3.
Differentiate terrestrial and aquatic habitats with an example of each. The verb is 'differentiate', LO-2's own.
Why the Bengal Tiger declined -- habitat loss from human activity. Environmental harm and its species consequence, LO-11.
What makes sacred groves protective -- community prohibition on cutting and harming. Community environmental protection, LO-11.

The consequence of habitat damage: organisms lose homes, food and resources, so biodiversity falls. A cause-to-consequence chain, LO-5; the item asks what follows, not what should be done, so not LO-11.
Purpose of the nature walk and the instructions given: carry a notebook to record observations (LO-4, recording observations during a survey) and respect living creatures (CG-SCI4).
Biodiversity and why it varies by region, with cactus and deodar as examples. Each example is a plant feature explained by its habitat, LO-5.
Full description of the herb/shrub/tree classification and each group's distinguishing features. LO-3's named category set at essay length.
The two venation types with an example each. A structural differentiation between reticulate and parallel, LO-2.
Taproot versus fibrous root and their correlation with venation. Taproot against fibrous is LO-2's own worked example.
Monocots versus dicots across seed, venation and root. The complete differentiation, LO-2.
Define adaptation and explain two animal examples in terms of how each aids survival in its habitat. LO-5's stated example verbatim.
What a habitat provides, what damage causes, and why biodiversity must be protected. The final clause is an argument for protection, LO-11.
Save Silent Valley as a success story, including the awareness campaigns people ran. LO-11 names spreading awareness explicitly.

Salim Ali listed birds, documented routes and habitats, and then acted to conserve high-diversity regions. LO-4 for the survey and recording of observations, LO-11 for the conservation measures that followed.
Plants A and B: classify by stem (LO-3), then infer venation and root type from the split seed (LO-2). Both halves are separately marked in parts (i) and (iii).
Rajasthan versus Ladakh camels, with each feature explained by its environment. Adaptation to habitat throughout, LO-5; the differences alone would be LO-2, but every part asks why.
Part (i) sorts fish and squirrel habitats as aquatic or terrestrial (LO-3); part (iii) asks what fish features adapt them to water (LO-5). Both are genuinely present.
Project Tiger, habitat loss, and why protecting habitats is crucial for biodiversity. The whole case study argues for protective action, LO-11.
Chickpea versus maize across seed structure, venation and root system. The monocot/dicot differentiation run in both directions, LO-2.
